title: Identity Provider (IdP)
explain: An identity provider is the one system that authenticates users, with password, MFA or passkeys, and vouches for their identity to other applications. Apps stop storing passwords and trust the IdP's signed answer, which gives single sign-on, central MFA and policy, and one place to disable a leaver. Three protocols to keep straight: SAML for enterprise SSO, OAuth 2.0 for delegated authorization, and OIDC for login on top of OAuth.
model:
Apps (relying parties) delegate authentication to the IdP, which acts as the *issuer* in [token minting](#/sd/f/token-minting) terms.

| Protocol | What it is | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| **SAML 2.0** | enterprise SSO into SaaS apps | XML **assertions** via browser redirects |
| **OAuth 2.0** | **delegated authorization**: the user lets an app call an API on their behalf | **access token** scoped to the grant; says nothing on its own about who the user is |
| **OpenID Connect** | thin **authentication** layer on OAuth 2.0 | **ID token**, a signed JWT (`sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `nonce`); "Log in with Google" |

**Authorization code flow (OIDC):**

```
App --redirect--> IdP (user authenticates) --redirect + one-time code--> App
App --back channel: code (+ client secret or PKCE)--> IdP token endpoint --> tokens
App validates the ID token --> creates its own session
```

Validate the ID token: signature against the IdP's published keys, `iss`, `aud` = your client id, `exp`, `nonce`.

**Limits:** your session or access token lives until its TTL, so offboarding bites at the next refresh unless you add revocation or back-channel logout. The IdP is a critical dependency: its outage blocks every login.

details.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization here, and which protocol does which?
details.a: Authentication answers who the user is; authorization answers what an app may do. OAuth 2.0 is authorization (an access token says the bearer may call an API). OIDC adds authentication on top, via the ID token. SAML does authentication (and attributes) with XML assertions.

details.q: A developer uses plain OAuth 2.0 and treats possession of a valid access token as proof of who logged in. Problem?
details.a: An access token is meant for an API and may have been issued to a different app. Use OIDC and validate the ID token (audience, issuer, nonce). The `aud` check ensures the token was issued for your app and not replayed from another.

details.q: What must you check on an ID token before trusting it?
details.a: The signature against the IdP's published keys (by `kid`), `iss` is the IdP you expect, `aud` is your client id, `exp` has not passed, and `nonce` matches the one you sent. A lookup in your own users table is not validation, and a first-time user would not be there anyway.

details.q: Why does the code exchange happen on a back channel rather than returning tokens in the redirect URL?
details.a: URLs land in browser history, logs and referrer headers. The code is single-use and useless alone; tokens only come on the direct app-to-IdP call, where the IdP can also authenticate the client (secret or PKCE). PKCE binds the code to the client that started the flow.

details.q: An employee is disabled at the IdP at 10:00. Their access token was issued at 09:50 with a 15-minute lifetime and the app verifies it by signature. How long can it still be used?
details.a: Until 10:05, five minutes after disablement, if the refresh token is revoked and no back-channel logout is configured. Shorter lifetimes shrink the window; immediate cut-off needs a revocation check or session revocation.

details.q: SAML vs OIDC: which would you pick?
details.a: OIDC for new apps, mobile and SPAs: JSON, JWTs, simple clients. SAML when an enterprise customer's IdP requires it; it is mature and common in B2B SaaS. Many products support both.

details.q: What does the IdP being a dependency mean for design?
details.a: Login is blocked if it is down, so keep existing sessions working through an outage, cache the IdP's signing keys (with rotation), and make the session lifetime a deliberate trade-off between offboarding speed and IdP load.

prompts.q: Explain what an IdP gives you and why apps use one.
points: Authenticates users in one place (password, MFA, passkey)
Apps trust the IdP's signed answer, no password storage
SSO, central policy, one place to disable a leaver
IdP is the issuer in token terms
OAuth 2.0: delegated authorization with access tokens, not identity
OIDC: identity layer on OAuth with an ID token
Access token vs ID token audiences

prompts.q: Walk through the OIDC authorization code flow and the ID token checks.
points: Redirect back with a one-time code
Back-channel exchange (secret or PKCE) for tokens
Validate signature, iss, aud, exp, nonce
Offboarding delay is bounded by token TTL unless revoked
